Project proposal · Week 5

Can synthetic images teach AI to check a shelter?

GenAI Shelter Validator: required objects, look-alikes and forbidden objects, found in one photo

Deep Generative Models for Visual Data

Shai Cohen, Gavriel Agibaev, Eliad Bicher and Almog Schwartzberg

Open with the question. Then say: we test whether generated images help a detector, and we measure on real photos only. Add the four team names on this slide before presenting.
Use case

Shelter checks are manual, and we found no image data

Why it matters

A shelter only protects people if it is ready when the alarm sounds.

Why it is hard

We found no labelled shelter images, and a fake extinguisher can pass a quick look.

How it is done today

A person walks the shelter against a written checklist. Slow and uneven.

Checklist source: the Home Front Command maintenance page for shared and public shelters. It is not a closed equipment list and does not cover the in-apartment safe room. Do not quote numbers about shelters unless a source is added.
Task and novelty

One photo in, visible objects out

Detect 10 object classes visible in a shelter photo. We check visible components, not certify a shelter.

  • A simple demo verdict: a shelter passes only if every required object is found and no forbidden object is found
  • Innovative: no dataset we found combines required, look-alike and forbidden objects
  • Hypothesis: generated data outperforms classical augmentation.

Search log (12 Nov 2026, EN + HE; Roboflow, Kaggle, Hugging Face, Zenodo, Mendeley, papers): only extinguisher sets (FireSafetyNet), gas cylinders (CylinDeRS) and tiny SUN "bomb shelter" scenes. No shelter set with look-alikes.

Input: one image. Output: a box and a class name for each object. Say the scope out loud: the task is checking visible components in the photo. The verdict on a whole shelter is a limited demonstration, measured on real test photos only, not a certification. Novelty is claimed only for the combination of the three roles in a shelter. Individual objects such as extinguishers exist in other datasets. SEARCH LOG (12 Nov 2026). Run with a web search engine, not by querying each platform's own search box, so say "web search" and not "we searched every database". The objects

Ten kinds of objects in three groups

Required (5)

  • Fire extinguisher
  • Vent opening with cover
  • “Shelter” sign
  • Light fixture
  • Drinking water, any container

Look-alikes (3)

  • Fake extinguisher
  • Vent without cover
  • Wrong sign

They look right at first glance, but are wrong.

Forbidden (2)

  • Gas cylinder
  • Mirror or framed glass

Any one makes the shelter invalid.

Source for the object list: [PLACEHOLDER]

This is the domain-expertise slide. Each class has a row in Data/objects_table.csv with appearance, context, size range, how to generate it, and a source. Be upfront: extinguisher and water are our choice. A gas cylinder anywhere in the image counts, we do not measure the three-metre distance. If Stable Diffusion cannot draw a believable Hebrew sign, two classes drop and eight remain.

Pipeline

From attribute list to detections in five steps

  1. 01

    Describe

    We write a list of shelter types, lighting, clutter and object variants.

    A scene list

  2. 02

    Collect

    100 to 150 photos from the web. We draw the boxes around objects by hand.

    Roboflow or CVAT

  3. 03

    Generate

    A adds objects. B changes capture conditions.

    Stable Diffusion

  4. 04

    Verify

    Filter bad images. Check quality by eye.

    Reliability report

  5. 05

    Tune and test

    Train 3 object-detection models on 5 different mixes of data. Score all of them on real test photos.

    T4 GPU

Method A: Stable Diffusion inpainting with ControlNet or GLIGEN places an object, a look-alike or a forbidden object inside a box, so the label comes for free. Method B changes how the photo was taken: dark, side light, glare, blur, noise, other background. The box stays put. The model choice for generation (SD 1.5 inpainting is the candidate) is still open.
Feasibility run

Can we generate the hard cases?

Each tile is a pair: the valid object on top and its look-alike below, on the same wall. Extinguisher: the fake is a red bottle with no hose and no pressure gauge, in the same bracket. Vent: generated locally with Stable Diffusion XL, modelled on public-shelter vents, a square panel with an exhaust fan high on the wall. There is no ladder under it on purpose: the State Comptroller report (p. 44) lists a fan in an escape hatch as a defect, so the valid case must read as a vent, not a hatch. First the wall with the panel, then inpainting replaces only the panel with an open opening, so the wall is identical and the box is known in advance. That is method A, and the label comes for free. The hard part is that the defect must stay visible at 512 by 512 pixels. The Hebrew sign is still to test, because Stable Diffusion does not reliably render Hebrew text.
Data

Real photos for testing, synthetic for training

Set Source Size Used for
Real photos Web, boxes by hand 100–150 Tune 80%, test 20%
Added objects Stable Diffusion paints in a missing object At least 100 per object type, together with the row below Training only
Method B Capture-condition edits 6 conditions Training only
Classical augmentation Dark, blur, noise, bright Same count as Method B Training (baseline run)

We hold back 10% of the training photos to know when to stop training. Test photos are always real.

The test set is small: 20 to 30 real photos, at least 10 with a look-alike and 5 with a forbidden object. Say this out loud, then show the risks slide. Web photos stay in Google Drive, not in GitHub (copyright). Synthetic counts follow an equal-size rule: mode 4 gets as many synthetic images as mode 2, mode 5 as many augmented images as mode 3, so a gain cannot come from more data.
Models and experiment

Three detectors, five modes

  • Three object-detection models: RT-DETR (Transformer-based), Faster R-CNN (CNN-based), and a third still to be chosen
  • Five setups: real photos only; plus AI-added objects; plus AI-changed conditions; plus both; plus simple edits (no AI)
  • Setups with extra images get matching numbers, so a gain cannot come from simply having more data
  • Same training settings in every run. 15 runs in total (3 models × 5 setups) on one T4 GPU
  • A ready-made model (Grounding-DINO) used as-is, with no training, as the lowest bar to beat
15 fine-tuning runs on a T4 GPU. Everything except the data is identical across runs. The open decisions: the third detector, how to load Faster R-CNN through the Hugging Face tools, ControlNet versus GLIGEN, and which SD model. Grounding-DINO is not one of the three models; it answers the course's fine-tuned versus off-the-shelf comparison. Mode 5 answers the question: why generative AI at all, when darkness and blur can be done classically?
Target KPIs

Four targets, measured on real photos only

  • +3 pp Overall detection score (mAP@50) vs. training on real photos only
  • +5 pp Share of small objects found
  • +5 pp Correct detections in photo conditions not seen in training, like very dark
  • −5 pp Fakes wrongly accepted as real (target to be confirmed)

pp = percentage points (60% to 63% is +3 pp). We also report, without targets: forbidden objects missed, how often the pass/fail verdict is right (F1), and two image-quality scores (FID, IS).

Targets are relative to fine-tuning on real photos only, on the real test set. Also state which method helped more (A or B), and that the trend must repeat in at least two models. Honest caveat: with 20 to 30 test photos, 3 points can be noise, and the PRD does not plan confidence intervals. IS is computed against ImageNet classes and FID needs far more images than we have real ones, so both are reported but are not proof of reliability. The human test (20 real, 20 synthetic, mixed) and the filter report are the real evidence.
Feedback requested

Five risks we want your view on

Week 9: generated data, EDA, baseline detector.

  • Test set is small: a 3-point gain may be noise
  • Web photos with look-alikes or forbidden objects may be rare
  • Almost no web photo shows all five required objects
  • The AI may not draw a readable Hebrew sign. If so, we drop two classes
  • Still open: a third object detector, and the tool that places objects (ControlNet or GLIGEN)
Close by asking for approval of the topic and for feedback on these five. Risk 3 in detail: the verdict rule needs every required object in one image, so there will be very few valid real test photos. The verdict is therefore measured on real test photos only, and composites (a web shelter photo with objects added synthetically) are a demo, not a result. The team does not photograph shelters at any point.
